title: Insider-trading oversight: requests, probes and outcomes
summary: The requests are well documented: at least ten letters from members of Congress (April 2025 to July 2026) asked the SEC, its inspector general, GAO, the Pentagon inspector general, DOJ, state attorneys general and a House committee to investigate trading around the tariff pause, Iran announcements, a reported attempted trade by Defense Secretary Hegseth's broker and the paid Truth API. Public responses are mostly silence: no SEC, inspector-general, state or House Financial Services investigation of these episodes has been announced, and House Democrats said in February 2026 they had no substantive SEC reply. Enforcement that did happen came through the CFTC and DOJ on prediction markets, mostly detected by the platforms: a soldier charged over Maduro bets, settled orders against a White House teleprompter operator and George Santos; the CFTC oil-futures probe is open with no charges after a reported referral retraction. No authority has identified a trader in the April 2025 or Iran-related trades or made any finding about Trump, his family or senior officials; that is not exoneration, and the letters are allegations, not findings. The STOCK Act names the President in the securities-law duty and tippees can be liable (our summary of the statute and case law), but the law has never been tested against a president and several gaps remain, while SEC enforcement staff fell 18% and CFTC staff about 21% below their ten-year average.

sub_claims.statement: Members of Congress asked the SEC, its inspector general and GAO to investigate trading around the 9 April 2025 tariff pause.
sub_claims.finding: Data: a burst of same-day SPY/QQQ call buying in the minutes before the 1:18 pm pause post, and a 21% rise in DJT shares after the 9:37 am 'THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT' post (see C58). Requests (letters read in full): on 10 April 2025 Rep. Maxine Waters and 20 other House Financial Services Democrats asked SEC Chair Paul Atkins, SEC Inspector General Deborah Jeffrey and Comptroller General Gene Dodaro for an immediate investigation of trading between Treasury Secretary Bessent's 6 April visit to Mar-a-Lago and the 9 April announcement, with preliminary findings by 18 April. On 11 April 2025 Senators Warren, Schumer, Kelly, Gallego, Schiff and Wyden asked Atkins whether Trump, Cabinet members, donors or other insiders engaged in insider trading or manipulation, whether the White House had contacted the SEC, and how staff departures affected its capacity, with answers by 25 April. Response: an SEC spokesperson declined to comment at the time. On 24 February 2026 Waters and Rep. Al Green wrote that 'It has been nearly a year and we have received no substantive response', that GAO 'does not have the authority to compel necessary information', and that Atkins, testifying earlier that month, 'appeared not to be aware of the facts and circumstances'. No SEC or SEC-IG investigation, finding or closure has been announced. No trader has been identified.
sources: https://www.banking.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/20250411 Letter to SEC re DJT Tariff Insider Trading.pdf

sub_claims.statement: Senators asked state attorneys general to investigate, and state authorities acted.
sub_claims.finding: The request is documented: on 11 April 2025 Senators Schumer, Warren, Schiff and Wyden wrote to the National Association of Attorneys General asking state offices to investigate whether 'President Trump, his family, members of his administration, or members of Congress engaged in insider trading, market manipulation, or any violations of the laws of your states' around the tariff changes (letter read in full). No state attorney general, comptroller or securities regulator was found to have opened an inquiry into the tariff trading or the paid Truth API, including under New York's Martin Act. State action found in this period concerns prediction markets as gambling (New York's suit against Polymarket, Arizona's criminal case against Kalshi) and, per search excerpts, executive orders in New York and Maryland barring state employees from using nonpublic information on prediction markets. Those are not investigations of the federal allegations.

sub_claims.statement: House Democrats asked the House Financial Services Committee to investigate the April 2025 trading itself.
sub_claims.finding: On 24 February 2026 Waters and Green asked Chairman French Hill to open a committee investigation into the identity of anyone who traded on, or manipulated markets around, the tariff pause, including call options in the 24 hours before the announcement and the 'DJT' post, and to refer any crimes to DOJ (letter read in full). No committee investigation or reply from the chairman was found.

sub_claims.statement: In 2026 senators asked the SEC and the Pentagon inspector general about trading before Iran and tariff announcements and about a broker for Defense Secretary Hegseth.
sub_claims.finding: Data and inference: reporting described index-futures and options spikes minutes before Iran-related posts; the Financial Times reported (30 March 2026) that Hegseth's Morgan Stanley broker contacted BlackRock in February about a multimillion-dollar investment in its Defense Industrials Active ETF before the 28 February strikes; the investment was not executed because the fund was not yet available to Morgan Stanley clients. Requests: Senators Mark Warner and Adam Schiff wrote on 2 April 2026 to SEC Chair Atkins and DoD Inspector General Platte Moring asking what each was doing to detect and investigate such trades, with a briefing and written response by 16 April (press release read in full). Sen. Warren wrote to Atkins on 20 April 2026 asking whether the SEC had investigated any attempted trading by Hegseth or associates, with answers by 15 May (letter read in full). Responses: the SEC declined to comment on the Warner-Schiff letter (CNBC excerpt). A Pentagon spokesperson denied that 'Secretary Hegseth [or] any of his representatives approached BlackRock about any such investment', while the FT stood by its reporting. No SEC or IG reply, investigation or finding was found. Separately, the Washington Post reported on 22 October 2026 (cited in the House Oversight memo) that Hegseth issued a memo barring defense personnel from using nonpublic information or prediction markets for personal gain.

sub_claims.statement: Lawmakers asked the SEC and DOJ to examine the paid Truth API, and the SEC investigated.
sub_claims.finding: Requests documented: Rep. Ritchie Torres wrote to Atkins in July 2026 (Axios, excerpt); Senators Warren and Schiff wrote on 28 July 2026 asking the SEC to 'immediately launch investigations' and for its legal analysis before the 1 August launch (letter read in full); Rep. Angie Craig asked DOJ and the SEC to investigate (search excerpt). Response: the SEC declined to comment to NPR and, per search excerpts, confirmed receipt of Torres's letter without saying whether it would act. TMTG says the product delivers 'publicly available Truth Social data' and called the letters partisan; CEO Kevin McGurn declined to comment on investigations in October 2026 (Axios excerpt). No SEC investigation has been announced. The only litigation is the First and Fifth Amendment suit by The Intercept and FPF (C58), not a securities case.

sub_claims.statement: The CFTC is investigating oil-futures trades placed before Trump's Iran posts.
sub_claims.finding: Data: large Brent/WTI positions placed minutes before the 23 March 2026 post and a reported ~$950M short before the 7 April ceasefire post (C58). Reuters and Bloomberg reported in April 2026 that the CFTC, with DOJ, was examining the trades on CME and ICE. Bloomberg reported on 13 October 2026, citing people familiar, that Mel Gunewardena, an adviser to Chair Selig, had market-surveillance staff retract a referral to the enforcement division; the CFTC declined to comment and Gunewardena did not respond. On 22 October 2026 Enforcement Director David Miller said at a New York conference that the agency had 'from the beginning' been probing the trading and the investigation 'remained open' (Reuters syndication, read in full). No trader has been named, no charge filed and no finding made as of mid-November 2026. Verdict is 'mostly-accurate' because the probe's existence rests on the director's statement and anonymous sourcing; its scope and progress are not public.

sub_claims.statement: Regulators have brought insider-trading cases over prediction-market bets on government information.
sub_claims.finding: Official actions (CFTC releases read in full): (1) 23 April 2026, CFTC civil complaint and SDNY indictment of Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke over Polymarket bets on the Maduro operation; the CFTC called it its first insider-trading case on event contracts and first use of the 'Eddie Murphy Rule'. The indictment has five counts (unlawful use of confidential government information, theft of nonpublic government information, commodities fraud, wire fraud, unlawful monetary transaction). He pleaded not guilty on 28 April 2026; trial was set for 7 December 2026. His motion to dismiss argues that his Polymarket contracts were event contracts, not swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act; prosecutors opposed it in August 2026 (ABC News), and no ruling was found by 16 November 2026. (2) 28 August 2026, settled CFTC order against Gabriel Perez, a White House teleprompter operator, who between December 2025 and February 2026 traded presidential 'mention' contracts on Kalshi using speeches he saw in advance: disgorgement of $107,539.02, a $65,000 penalty discounted for cooperation, and a three-year trading ban. Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt had confirmed the probe on 16 July 2026, said he was on unpaid leave and that she knew of no other staff under investigation. (3) 31 July 2026, settled order against former Rep. George Santos ($17,569.98 disgorgement plus a $17,500 penalty, about $35,000) for manipulating a State of the Union attendance contract through misleading posts about his own attendance; this is a manipulation case, not insider trading. Also a 27 May 2026 complaint against a Google employee (not government). In each case the platform (Kalshi or Polymarket) detected and reported the trades. None of these cases involves Trump, his family or a policy-level official.

sub_claims.statement: Congress and the prediction-market platforms investigated insider trading on those platforms.
sub_claims.finding: House Oversight Chairman James Comer (R) opened an investigation on 22 May 2026 with letters to Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan and Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour, expanded on 29 September 2026 to Hyperliquid Labs, Crypto.com and PredictIt. A staff memorandum dated 13 November 2026 (read in full) says the committee received about 1,700 pages and five bipartisan briefings; four of five platforms cooperated, and Hyperliquid said it did not 'possess the types of records and information' requested. The memo credits the platforms with detecting most reported cases and recommends legislation restricting federal personnel from event contracts. It identifies no new trader and does not address securities or futures trades around presidential announcements. Rep. Casten, Rep. Lieu and 14 other House Democrats asked Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche on 12 May 2026 to prioritise prediction-market insider-trading prosecutions and questioned the July 2025 closure of the Polymarket probe (letter read in full); no DOJ reply was found. The Senate adopted S.Res. 708 on 30 April 2026 barring senators and staff from prediction-market trading.

sub_claims.statement: The executive branch and the Office of Government Ethics responded with rules or guidance.
sub_claims.finding: Documented: the White House Management Office emailed staff on 24 March 2026 that trading prediction or futures contracts on nonpublic information breaks ethics rules and can be criminal (C58); the White House disciplined the teleprompter operator; the CFTC Enforcement Division issued a prediction-markets advisory on 25 February 2026 citing CEA section 6(c)(1) and Rule 180.1; and the Defense Department issued a memo in October 2026 (Washington Post, via the House Oversight memo). Not found: any new OGE legal advisory or rule on prediction markets or on trading around presidential announcements. CREW wrote on 18 May 2026 to Eric Ueland as OGE acting director (senators wrote the same day that, according to records received by Congress, his acting service had ended in early Dec 2025 and OGE had no acting head; Acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling was named acting director on 23 June 2026), to work with the President on a ban for political appointees and senior career staff (letter read in full); no OGE response was found.

sub_claims.statement: Enforcement staffing and policy at the SEC, CFTC and DOJ changed in ways that bear on capacity to investigate.
sub_claims.finding: Documented (no motive asserted). SEC: GAO-26-107813 (March 2026, read in part) found about 18% of SEC employees left in FY2025, mostly through voluntary incentives; Enforcement went from 1,305 staff to 235 fewer (18%), Trading and Markets lost 22%; the agency had about 4,000 employees in January 2026, which GAO says is lower than its average full-time-equivalent workforce in any year since 2014 (Table 2 and the highlights re-read in the audit: Enforcement 109 voluntary incentives + 54 deferred resignation + 72 other attrition = 235 of 1,305). The SEC brought 313 cases in FY2025 versus 431 the year before (White & Case, excerpt); Better Markets, an advocacy group, calls it a ten-year low; the SEC says earlier resources were 'misapplied' to 'run up numbers'. The commission rescinded the Enforcement Director's delegated authority to issue formal orders in March 2025 (White & Case, excerpt), Enforcement Director Margaret Ryan resigned on 16 March 2026 after under seven months (C52), and the SEC has sought comment on 'foundational and existential aspects' of the Consolidated Audit Trail used to reconstruct trading (Better Markets). CFTC: OPM data show 21% fewer staff at end-2025 than the prior ten-year average and nearly 80% fewer enforcement actions in 2025 than the decade average (NPR, read in full); the CFTC says departures were mostly voluntary retirements and it plans about 100 hires by end-2026; Chair Selig is the sole commissioner. GAO agreed to review CFTC staffing at Sen. Warren's request, starting December 2026. DOJ: a 7 April 2025 memo by Deputy AG Todd Blanche disbanded the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team; NBC reported on 11 March 2025, citing three anonymous sources, that the Public Integrity Section would be cut to about half a dozen employees and stop directly handling prosecutions.

sub_claims.statement: Insider-trading law reaches a president, officials, their families and friends.
sub_claims.finding: Securities: STOCK Act section 9(b) (Pub. L. 112-105, read in full) affirms executive-branch employees are 'not exempt' from section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 and adds Exchange Act section 21A(h), under which each executive-branch employee owes a duty of trust and confidence to the government and citizens for material nonpublic information 'derived from such person's position'; the Act's definition of executive-branch employee expressly includes the President and Vice President. Under Dirks v. SEC and Salman v. United States, a tipper is liable if he discloses for a personal benefit, which includes a gift of information to a relative or friend, and a tippee who knows of the breach is liable when trading. So, on our reading of the statute and case law (no court has applied it to these facts), officials, and family or friends who trade on a tip, are covered on paper. Commodities: CEA section 4c(a)(3)-(4) (7 U.S.C. 6c) bars any 'employee or agent of any department or agency of the Federal Government' from using government information that has not been made public, 'in his personal capacity and for personal gain', to trade futures, options on futures, off-exchange options or swaps, or from imparting it for personal gain to help another trade; makes a person who 'knowingly' uses such imparted information liable; and makes it unlawful for 'any person' to steal, convert or misappropriate such information and trade on it (section 4c(a)(4)(C), the provision the CFTC calls the 'Eddie Murphy Rule'). The statute text was re-read in the audit. The CFTC treats event contracts as swaps; Van Dyke's pending motion to dismiss disputes that, and no court has ruled. CFTC Rule 180.1 is modelled on 10b-5. Gaps and limits: (a) a public post is not a tip, and several professors (Coffee, Pritchard, Seyhun; PolitiFact, excerpt) say the 9 April post itself is unlikely to violate insider-trading law, while aides who traded would face STOCK Act exposure; (b) whether the President is an 'employee or agent of any department or agency' under the CEA provision is untested. Our own reading, not a source's: section 4c(a)(3) borrows the STOCK Act's definitions only for Members and employees of Congress and judicial officers and employees, so the STOCK Act's express inclusion of the President does not carry over to the 'department or agency' phrase; the 'any person' theft provision in 4c(a)(4)(C) has no such limit; (c) the OGE rule on nonpublic information (5 CFR 2635.703) and 18 U.S.C. 208 do not apply to the President or Vice President (5 CFR 2635.102(h); 18 U.S.C. 202(c)); (d) after Kelly, the Second Circuit in Blaszczak (2022) held confidential agency regulatory information is not 'property' for Title 18 wire and securities fraud, narrowing criminal routes outside the Exchange Act and CEA; (e) DOJ policy (OLC, 2000) bars indicting a sitting president, and Trump v. United States (2024) gives immunity for official acts but not unofficial ones. John Coates, a former SEC general counsel under Biden, argues the STOCK Act makes the President a fiduciary and that selling early access to official announcements could breach it, with a five-year limitations period; TMTG rejects that theory. No court has applied any of these provisions to a president.

sub_claims.statement: Any authority has found that Trump, his family or a senior official traded on, or tipped others about, nonpublic information around these announcements.
sub_claims.finding: No. Through mid-November 2026 no regulator, prosecutor, inspector general, court or congressional committee has identified a trader in the 9 April 2025 options burst, the Iran oil-futures trades or the Iran-strike prediction-market bets, and none has made a finding about Trump, his family, Cabinet members or senior appointees. The only government personnel sanctioned or charged are a soldier (charged, pleads not guilty) and a White House teleprompter operator (settled civil order). The absence of an investigation or finding is not exoneration: the SEC has not said whether it looked, the CFTC oil probe is open, and requests for answers have gone unanswered in public. Equally, the letters are allegations and requests, not findings.

corrections: Claimed in the 10 April 2025 and 24 February 2026 House letters: Trump said 'he made $2.5 million today'. The record shows: the Oval Office remark was 'two-and-a-half billion' (Charles Schwab) and '$900 million' (Roger Penske), Trump's own claims about paper gains (C58). The letters cite a social-media post for the quotation.

Claimed (House Oversight letter of 29 September 2026 and memo of 13 November 2026): a Hyperliquid short was established 'within minutes' of an October 2025 tariff announcement. The record shows: the article both documents cite (Bank Syz, republished by Investing.com) describes a build-up that began about 28-30 hours before the 20:50 UTC post (account funded 16:39 UTC on 9 October) and continued until about 20:49 UTC, and its summary says the position was 'opened 30 hours before'. 'Within minutes' fits the last additions, not the opening. An earlier version of this check called the memo's wording wrong; it is incomplete rather than wrong. No trader has been identified (see C101).
The White House teleprompter operator's profit was first reported as 'close to $100,000'; the CFTC order puts it at $107,539.02, with a $65,000 penalty (about $172,500 in total).

The DOJ memo disbanding the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team (7 April 2025) was written by Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, not Attorney General Bondi, though it is often attributed to her.

2026-11-16 (audit): the George Santos order is for manipulation of a contract on his own attendance, not insider trading; the Van Dyke indictment has five counts; the CFTC complaint and DOJ give slightly different profit figures (more than $404,000 versus about $409,881).

2026-11-17: Claimed: CREW's 18 May 2026 letter went to 'OGE Acting Director Eric Ueland'. CREW did address it that way, but senators wrote the same day that his acting service had ended in early Dec 2025 and that OGE had no acting head; Keith Sonderling was named acting director on 23 June 2026 (C109).
denials_and_context: The White House said in April 2025 that the 'great time to buy' post was meant to reassure markets, and spokesmen have called suggestions that officials traded on inside information 'baseless and irresponsible' (C58).
A Pentagon spokesperson denied that Hegseth or any representative approached BlackRock; the trade was never executed.
TMTG says the Truth API sells faster access to public data and that critics 'invented a new theory of insider trading'; it called the senators' letter partisan.

The SEC says its enforcement decline reflects a deliberate refocus away from 'misapplied' resources; Atkins called senators' enforcement statistics 'wrong' in February 2026 before the SEC's own figures showed the decline.

The CFTC says staff losses were mostly voluntary retirements, that it is hiring, and that the oil-trades probe has been open 'from the beginning'. It does not confirm or deny investigations, and the referral-retraction account rests on anonymous sources.
Kalshi and Polymarket say they police insider trading; the House Oversight memo credits them with detecting most known cases.

Several law professors (Coffee, Pritchard, Seyhun) say Trump's public post is unlikely to be insider trading in itself; others (Woody, Jones, Coates) say an investigation is warranted or that the Truth API raises STOCK Act issues. Coates disclosed that he served at the SEC under Biden.
Silence is not exoneration and allegations are not findings: congressional letters set out questions and inferences from timing; none identifies a trader.

Source limits: the 2 April 2026 Warner-Schiff PDF could not be parsed (its press release was read in full); CRS report LSB11406, the CLS Blue Sky 'Shadow SEC' statement, PolitiFact, White & Case, Axios and Bloomberg could not be read directly, so those points rest on excerpts or secondary coverage.

changes: Hyperliquid correction rewritten: the memo's and letter's 'within minutes' and their cited article's '30 hours' describe the end and the start of the same build-up (16:39 UTC on 9 October to 20:49 UTC on 10 October). The earlier correction said 'within minutes' was wrong; it is incomplete. Now consistent with C101.

GAO: Enforcement 1,305 staff, 235 departures (18%), Trading and Markets 22%, agency-wide 871 (about 18%) confirmed; 'lowest since 2014' reworded to GAO's comparison with the average workforce since 2014.

Law: CEA 4c(a)(3)-(4) restated from the text (personal-gain element, knowing use by recipients, 'any person' theft provision); the CFTC's treatment of event contracts as swaps flagged as disputed in Van Dyke's motion; the researcher's readings (tippee coverage, the President under the CEA) marked as our reading, with the textual reason. STOCK Act sections 2(3)(B)(i) and 9(b)/21A(h) confirmed as stated.
Prediction-market enforcement: Santos order is manipulation, not insider trading; Van Dyke five counts, motion to dismiss and August 2026 opposition, trial still set for 7 December 2026.

Upheld: Blanche authored the 7 April 2025 NCET memo; the retracted CFTC referral rests on anonymous sources (Bloomberg) with the enforcement director's on-record statement that the probe is open; no charges, no SEC action and no finding about Trump, his family or senior officials through 16 Nov 2026.
